newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin win would be soured by "cohabitation" clash.
newsitem.headline: Jospin win would be soured by "cohabitation" clash.

text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who has dragged his party out of the stifling shadow of the late President Francois Mitterrand, will score a bitter-sweet triumph if he wins Sunday's runoff election vote.

Victory in the parliamentary poll would commit him to enforced "cohabitation", or power-sharing, not only with his conservative foe President Jacques Chirac but also with possibly fractious Communist and Green partners.
The 59-year-old Jospin's highest state office to date was a stint as education minister under Mitterrand, the first Socialist head of state of the Fifth Republic.
But the tall, lean professorial figure has plenty of experience of managing political rivalry, as leader of a Socialist Party plagued by infighting in the wake of Mitterrand's death in January 1996.
From Chirac's standpoint, Jospin would be much more difficult to work with than outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe, the president's most loyal and longest-serving political associate.
Jospin's steady nerves and cool manner would be assets in fencing with the impulsive president, as well as with leftist allies hostile to plans for a single European currency.
Despite a lack of charisma, Jospin has in the election campaign embodied voter resentment at Juppe's authoritarian style, record unemployment and corruption in the ruling centre-right coalition.
He is friendly and witty in private, easily slipping into slang, but on the campaign trail Jospin refused to play to the gallery.
At rallies, he stands stiffly and reads his speeches as if he were still a university lecturer, in a strained, metallic tone. Television crews are hard-pressed to find a short, sharp sound-bite.
Photographers complain that snapping him is like trying to capture the invisible man because his generous silver curls bounce light off his face and erases all contrast.

The son of a schoolteacher, Jospin attended France's elite National Administration College (ENA) -- widely criticised for producing technocratic clones -- and joined the Foreign Ministry, before dropping out to become an economics lecturer.
He describes himself as "warm, straightforward and simple" and says he knows how to have fun, but concedes: "A sense of modesty cramps and confines me a little."
A television puppet satire show long portrayed him as "Yoyo", a well-meaning simpleton based on Enid Blyton's "Noddy", driving round in a toy car seeking ideas.

Jospin suggested that Chirac's decision to call a snap election masked a secret agenda by the centre-right -- a swing to "hardline capitalism", more austerity to qualify for a single currency and an amnesty to pardon political sleaze.
The ruling coalition has spluttered denials but failed to produce convincing reasons for the election. Chirac said it was intended to give France a "new elan" to help join a single European currency.
Jospin set his campaign tone the day before Chirac's formal announcement of the dissolution. Anticipating the step, he called it "an admission of failure" when an election was not due until 1998.

In a prime-time television interview, he made a key promise -- if he won, he would not impose further austerity to qualify France for a single European currency, a vote-winner in a country that only narrowly approved the Maastricht Treaty on European union in a cliffhanger 1992 referendum.
The left scored a stunning upset last Sunday by winning most votes in the first round, and the electorate looked tempted to force Chirac to share power with Jospin.

Such "cohabitation" would tie France's main political forces into a straitjacket for at least one year -- the legal period before Chirac could next play the dissolution card -- and possibly until the end of the president's seven-year term in 2002.
Born in 1937 in Meudon south of Paris, to a family of ardent Socialists, he had a strict Protestant upbringing in an overwhelmingly Roman Catholic country.
